text.title: Portfolio EVM Rollup Method Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every portfolio EVM rollup MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Portfolio PV, EV and AC MUST be computed by summing each project's PV, EV and AC in one reporting currency at one data date. Portfolio SPI = sum(EV) / sum(PV) and portfolio CPI = sum(EV) / sum(AC). Averaging per-project SPI or CPI, simple or weighted, is forbidden.

rationale.source: PMI Practice Standard for Earned Value Management (2nd ed., 2011); ANSI/EIA-748 EVMS guidelines

rule.rationale: A $50k project at CPI 1.30 and a $2M project at CPI 0.80 average to 1.05: a healthy portfolio that is losing money. Indices are ratios of money; only the money sums. The rollup exists to show the director the real margin, and an averaged index hides exactly the project large enough to matter.

rule.statement: Every project contributes PV, EV and AC as of the same data date, taken from its week-grain ledger export (file and export timestamp recorded per project). A project whose latest ledger entry is older than the data date by more than one reporting period is marked `stale`, excluded from the aggregate, and listed separately with its BAC; its last values are never carried forward silently.

rationale.source: PMI Practice Standard for Earned Value Management: data date (time-now) discipline

rule.rationale: Mixing a project reported on the 30th with one reported on the 12th produces an aggregate for a date that never existed. The usual shape of the incident is one PM on leave: last month's numbers are copied forward, the portfolio CPI looks flat, and the 15% overrun that started three weeks ago reaches the executive review a month late.

rule.statement: The artefact records the EV measurement method per project: milestone weight, 0/100, 50/50, physical percent complete, apportioned effort, or level of effort (LOE). Fixed-bid projects earn EV on accepted milestones or deliverables at contract value, never on self-reported percent complete. LOE work is summed and shown separately from discrete work in the rollup, not blended into the portfolio SPI.

rationale.source: ANSI/EIA-748 earned value techniques; Fleming & Koppelman, Earned Value Project Management

rule.rationale: Self-reported percent complete on a $1M fixed-bid runs at 90% for four months and nobody can falsify it. LOE earns value by the passage of time, so its SPI is 1.0 by construction and dilutes every real schedule slip it is blended with. Naming the method per project is what lets a reviewer challenge the number.

rule.statement: The per-project block carries, for each project: BAC, PV, EV, AC, SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC, VAC, EV method, data date, currency, and the EAC formula used (BAC / CPI, or AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI), or a bottom-up estimate flagged as such). A row missing any field is rejected by the validator.

rationale.source: PMI Practice Standard for Earned Value Management (formulas for SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC, VAC)

rule.rationale: EAC is the number the executive acts on and it changes by 20% depending on the formula. A table that shows EAC without naming the formula lets a PM pick the flattering one each month. The fixed field set is also what makes month-over-month diffs mechanical instead of a re-read.

rule.statement: The rollup states the numeric thresholds that escalate a project to the executive review (the portfolio owner's policy sets them; a common shape is SPI or CPI below 0.90, or cost variance beyond 10% of BAC). Every project beyond a threshold carries a one-line variance narrative with cause and corrective action; projects inside the thresholds carry no narrative.

rationale.source: ANSI/EIA-748 variance analysis and reporting thresholds; PMI Practice Standard for Earned Value Management

rule.rationale: Executives read three red rows, not fourteen paragraphs. Without a written threshold, which projects get a narrative depends on which PM is loudest, and the quiet 0.85 CPI project gets a green paragraph about "good team morale". The threshold also stops the opposite failure: writing defensive prose for a project that is fine.

rule.statement: Portfolio SPI and CPI are shown as a trend over at least the last three monthly data dates alongside the current value, per project and in aggregate. A single-point index with no history is rejected.

rationale.source: Christensen & Heise (1993), CPI stability research; Fleming & Koppelman, Earned Value Project Management

rule.rationale: Cumulative CPI tends to stabilise once a project is a fifth of the way through, which means a CPI that is still moving is itself the finding: a drop from 0.98 to 0.91 to 0.86 is a project that will not recover, while a flat 0.91 is a known cost. A snapshot cannot tell those two apart, and the executive decision (re-baseline, descope, or accept) depends on which one it is.

rule.statement: If any weighting other than the plain currency sum is applied (strategic weight, margin weight, client-tier weight), the artefact prints the weight per project and the policy document it comes from, and shows the unweighted currency-sum SPI, CPI and EAC next to the weighted figures. Weighted-only reporting is forbidden.

rationale.source: Portfolio weighting policy prerequisite (AGENTS.md); widely established practice in portfolio reporting

rule.rationale: A weight nobody can see is a lever for making the number green. The moment a strategic multiplier of 1.5 on the flagship project is discovered after a bad quarter, every previous rollup is retroactively worthless. Printing both numbers costs one column and removes the argument.

rule.statement: The executive summary states portfolio EAC against portfolio BAC in currency, the resulting VAC, and for fixed-bid projects the implied margin (contract value minus EAC) per project and in total. Indices without the money figures are rejected.

rationale.source: PMI Practice Standard for Earned Value Management (EAC, VAC); this methodology's purpose statement (real margin at the monthly review)

rule.rationale: A portfolio at SPI 0.97 and CPI 0.96 reads as fine until the same data says EAC exceeds contract value by $400k on two fixed-bid projects. The executive owns margin, not ratios; a rollup that makes them do the multiplication is a rollup that does not get read.
